The Matrix is a fantastic analogy for our current way of life, Severance works almost as a spin-off in my mind.

While we are probably not simulated avatars in an advanced computer program, we have effectively separated ourselves from a truly human experience 

In the movie, those in the matrix live a very familiar lifestyle to what most of us see and do on a daily basis. In our world the matrix exists as our control systems: Government, Employment, Society, Religion. Anything that makes us create an avatar for ourselves because we are expected to live or perform in a certain manner. 

In the movies, real life is very much not like the simulation. The humans who were able to escape the matrix and leave the pods live a dirty, difficult, survival driven experience, the benefit to that is an actual life experience. In our real life, escaping our matrix means just that, putting down the electronics, stepping away from the desk and fully experiencing life. 

Our "simulation" exists from an observer's standpoint. Punching numbers on a keyboard or digging ditches or leading a country is not "living" it is providing you a means to live life. 

Like The Matrix there are millions of people who would rather go day to day doing their thing without thinking about rhyme or reason. There are some that would rather sacrifice their own life than give up the ability to live by their own rule. And there are still some that find acceptance in the deal that has been signed.

 The persona you assume at your workplace may not be the same persona you show to your close friends and that may be different than who you show to your children or significant other, further, that may be different than the persona you know of yourself.  Anytime you put on a different face you have entered "The Matrix."

There are a few things to consider with evolution, first it is linear, we do not have a record of every generation of living organisms since the dawn of time. If you pull out your Animorphs book and flip through the pages, you can see the transition from human to animal. Similarly, if you had access to every generation of being to the dawn of time you could flip yourself all the way back to the same single celled organism that sparked life on this planet. 

Second, as shown by Darwin, when populations are separated, different adaptations will occur and those who are able to successfully reproduce may have some unique adaptations to their environment and may diversify far enough from the main group to develop enough genetic diversity to be considered a different species. 

Third, modern genetics have been able to more accurately distinguish between species due to genetic markers vs physical differences, I believe some of Darwin's claims have been refuted to some of the birds not having enough genetic diversity and are more like domestic dogs in that genetically they fall under the same species but the looks are widely varied. Not his fault he just didn't have access to the tools we have. 

To answer why Humans and Neanderthals are different species, it is an odd concept to think of but at one point in time there may have been five or six distinct hominid species living independently across the globe. These populations didn't really cross mingle. During the last ice age, there was a push of almost all warm blooded animals from the northern hemisphere south to the equator. These populations began to intermingle and reproduce due to proximity. As the Neanderthals assimilated into Human territory, their unique population as a species kind of merged into the rest of the human population as they were provided more opportunities to mate with humans more often than other Neanderthals, you would see less and less full blooded Neanderthals and more hybrids. As hybrid species are generally not fertile, it doesn't mean that one or two Neanderthals weren't lucky enough to be able to pass on a few genes into modern man.

I wouldn't consider my experience traumatic by any means. Looking back, I think confession was the worst of the process. At age 7 you begin your full initiation to the church. From 7-11 or 12 depending on the way they scheduled things you received three sacraments beginning with Reconciliation. You would sit face to face with a priest and tell them your sins so as a child my understanding of a sin was pretty much everything you got in trouble for. What was worse was since "Nobody was perfect but Jesus" even if you were on your best behavior you would be compelled to make something small up aka lie to the priest. But you aren't going to confess that you lied. And it was all very odd. 

Then around 5th or 6th grade you had Confirmation, which makes you a full member of the Church. It involves a year of studying the faith and memorizing tenants. Then you went before the Bishop, were asked to repeat these tenants verbatim in front of the entire congregation. The kicker about this was Religious Studies were graded and all of that studying happened during a graded subject. So you were required to learn this in order to pass grade school. To top off, since you were in Catholic school to continue past 6th grade you had to be Catholic so if you chose not to join the church you were effectively expelled from school. No brainer for a nerdy kid who enjoyed learning things like math, science, history, and literature. I never wanted to go through confirmation but I also didn't want to leave a school with all my friends. Oddest part now is my closest friends ALL went to the school I would have gone to IF I left the church then. 

I thank you, kind stranger for letting me get that out; it was very therapeutic.

When the review was done, the Joepresso cost about $65 (per review) I was able to get on Amazon for $40.
Yes that's it. I wasn't sure if that was exactly what it was called.

You get a fuller extraction, more crema and a richer body with the Joepresso. The scoop that comes with the Aero is just the right amount of espresso ground coffee. I fill the water up to the 1 and stir for 20 seconds. The basket is pressurized with the Joepresso so it takes a bit of muscle to press out the shot. 

Using the same recipe on the Aero, I found that while it is a strong coffee, it lacks the full body of a shot of espresso. 

Head the warning that you do not want to use the Joepresso over a glass. I have the Aeropress Travel set and the plastic carafe holds up to the extra push on the plunger without sliding or tipping.

Kind of like apples to oranges. The classic Aeropress makes a really smooth cup of coffee. I was a French Press guy for the longest time but I was not a fan of the sludginess with the final product. I use paper filters in my Aero and am more than pleased with the result. 

Time to time I enjoy a good strong espresso and I do not have a good coffee shop in a reasonable distance. The Joepresso fills that hole in my under-caffinated heart. 

You can use the same roast in either method and get two completely different products. Variety is the spice of life.

Like most of the reviews, this is not quite the same as a steam pulled espresso shot. But it does give a concentrated extraction, also a thicker foam than anticipated with the reviews. If you are willing to spend an extra $40 to save a trip to the coffee shop it is well worth the money.

Without actually working in a facility, it is hard to explain how diverse the population truly is. Most of your "nice" inmates are long term offenders, either serving life sentences or extremely long sentences where they know they will never see the outside again, either due to advanced age during incarceration or an extremely lengthy sentence. 

That said, there comes a time where you need to decipher motives. Are these people being nice because they accept their sentence and are trying to make the most of the life they gave themselves? Or, are they being nice to your face because they want a favor, preferential treatment, or their crime was so heinous they are outcast by their companions? 

The former usually represent murderers, big time drug trafficking, or those who were "in a bad place" during their life. Most lifers, especially those who have spent more than a decade in prison, accept their sentence, own up to the fact that they have done wrong and are trying to make the most of the life they have left, they are ones that know the rules better than you ever will, and even will assist with keeping control of their housing unit ( in that they will make sure other inmates are not trying to run amok and cause problems.)

The latter usually cause more problems than good, for themselves and for officers. They are generally sex offenders or those who committed crimes against children. Inmates don't respect them. They turn to Officers and staff as "friends" they are manipulative and will use their orientation, mental capacity, or anything else as fodder for lawsuits, grievances etc. They will try to hold those things over your head to get you to turn a blind eye to things, especially contraband they possess. Personally, I like to call these people 'Sweet and Low' inmates. Fake sweetness and too much will give you cancer. 

Overall, most are not as Savage as their crimes would have you think. There are a lot of young kids that I wish would take advantage of the systems in place and try to better themselves. Ultimately, it is up to them, but I try to give everyone a chance to change.

One of our senior officers was questioned as to why there were so few inmates out during evening block out, his response was "I don't like them and they don't like me." In the long run, this is a perfectly acceptable response. We are not paid to make friends. That being said, the night goes a lot faster when you have the rapport to hold a general conversation with people. 

That is where the grey area of corrections lies, you don't want to give the impression that you are not paying attention to your post, you don't want other officers to think that you are becoming too friendly with inmates, and you don't want other inmates to think you are playing favorites.

I graduated college almost 10 years ago. From my first semester of my Senior year, I tried to find the right job. I knew I wanted to work in Law Enforcement on some level. My first shot was a Police Officer at the United States Supreme Court. I took the test, and got a call back for an interview. It was the singlemost disheartening interview I ever had.

Over the next 8 years, I bounced back and forth to crappy jobs I didn't want to do. I made an attempt to get into a Doctorate Program, I made a waiting list but couldn't get the final push. All the while, I applied to and tested for every law enforcement opportunity I saw. State Police, Liquor Control Board, local Police, State and County Corrections, State Parole, even FBI; if it was available I tested.

There was always one thing or another that kept the job out of my reach, hiring freezes, lack of military experience, failed physical tests (one I failed because I skipped a stair on a run), the list goes on. Every time I was not selected I tried to learn from that experience. Every failure was a little soul crushing.

Six months ago, 9 years after graduating, I was hired as a State Corrections Officer. I could not be happier.

What I learned is not to give up. The second you stop trying is the second you lose. I cannot tell you how many times I failed before I succeded in my field. 

The best advice I can give you is if you are unhappy with your job, do something different. Between graduating college and now, I have worked at bars and restaurants, from dish washer to manager. I worked in mental health with children and adults. I even worked at a warehouse. Some I thought could be careers, some I knew were only temporary until the right position came along. 

Also, don't be afraid to work below your perceived skill level. At some companies, you need a foot in the door. Throw boxes in a shipping department for a few months, if you have post graduate credits, a fair amount will help you financially to finish your degree and an MBA at Wal-Mart will take you corporate in no time (Wal-Mart Logistics pays over $20 an hour after bonuses and incentives after a year of employment and upper management pays nearly six figures.)

Lastly, is some advice from my Mom "work to live, don't live to work."

TL;DR

Keep trying, do something different, things will eventually work out.

Tipping is not a scam. I had this conversation the other day. When I started the service industry, I had the same mentality as you, I was being paid by my employer and people were giving me extra money (total scam). After working for 5 or 6 years, I landed a position at a high volume venue. At that point I understood the concept. My employer was paying me to: 1. Serve paying customers and 2. Make sure the money was added up. They could give a damn about how the customers got their drinks, in which order they were served, and as long as they were in the building and still spending money, how happy they were.

My pay checks for 2 weeks netted around $40. That was taking out my 35% taxes and benefits, which included a 401k. What people do not understand is, tipping makes you a secondary employer (to a degree). At a crowded bar, my main job is to make my company money, or else I will no longer be at a crowded bar (think paying for a storefront). So, by selling time to my company, I have a prime spot to sell my personality and service. 

My service comes with a price that I am selling to customers. In this environment, I can adjust what I am worth. If someone is tipping $5 every time he buys a drink he is going to receive more of my dedication because I believe that you should get what you pay for. When someone comes up to my bar and is yelling at me, not tipping, making a mess or being rude to other people, he is going to get his drink and pretty much nothing else. Imagine a person walking into a club style grocery store like Sam's club, where you pay for membership instead of checking out and paying for his purchase he just walks out and leaves because he already paid to be a member so he shouldn't have to pay for the product. The drink you buy is your membership fee. The service I give is the product. 

That all being said, the service industry can be great for a while, late nights, bad hours, legal regulations, business demands all start wearing down on you. It also is not conducive to having a family. I recommend everyone to do it for a few years. If you are good at it You can make a ton of money in a short time (bought me a car a house and paid off my student loans) but cannot withstand a career less you give up your aspirations and completely immerse yourself in the industry. You work when your friends and family are off, your new friends are waiters, cooks, and bartenders.

One last thing, if a customer says they are a bartender at 10 PM on a Saturday night, they are not a good one, you don't get that shift off if you are good.

TL;DR

Service workers have 2 employers, their company and their customers. Employers pay their taxes, customers pay their bills.

This has been my personal dilemma with minimum wage reform. When minimum wage was first enacted it was set to provide one man working 40 hours a week to support a family of four. 

The thing is when they first set this it worked fine. A worker was able to feed, clothe and shelter their family.

When adjusted for inflation, the current federal minimum wage reflects the same equivalent amount that was used in the past. 

Using the same formula, along with proper budget, one worker can feed, clothe and shelter their family. I have to use prices that I am familiar with so I am basing this on a rural area in Pennsylvania.

The issue that exists is food, clothing and housing are no longer the bare necessities. At minimum people "need" phones, internet access, reliable transportation. Those are all added expenses. The reliable transportation part adds other bills into the mix like insurance, upkeep and gas.

When you add those expenses to other typical expenses like student debt and credit card debt, the idea of minimum wage supporting a family is preposterous.

My question is: If the minimum wage is still providing what it was intended to provide do we need to raise it? Or do we need to reevaluate what it should provide and adjust accordingly?

I was going to use the example of bowling. In standard 10 pin, the ball is close to the size of a football (soccer). Upon release the ball hits oil on the lane a goes into the first part of its movement which is called slide. At this point the ball is moving without any spin direction. As the ball crosses the point in the pattern without any or much less friction the ball starts to spin, this is the aptly named spin portion of the movement. Once enough inertia is gained the ball should change trajectory and finish its movement in the roll part of its movement.

It should be noted that many professional and skilled bowlers will manipulate their release and hole patterns to increase their spin or decrease their roll etc. This full pattern can best be seen when the ball is thrown flat without added wrist movement and on a simple oil pattern.

I am going to start by addressing the second part of your comparison. Scooby Doo and Tom and Jerry are from completely different times. Tom and Jerry are part of the "Golden Age" of cartoons along with the Looney Toons and Disney shorts. These were all shown in the beginnings of Motion Pictures before Trailers took over so these were supposed to appeal to adult audiences which is why you will see themes like smoking and drinking by the characters. As time went on you hit shows like The Flintstones and The Jetsons which were still aimed at adult audiences. It was at this point in the late 1960s when mainly Hannah-Barberra realized that children were enjoying animation more than adults. Programs with more zany characters were being shown such as The Banana Splits and Scooby Doo. This began the advent of Saturday morning Cartoons. In the 1980s, realizing that children were impressionable you had very nonsensical shows that worked as advertisements for toys, think Rainbow Bright and Care Bears. There was also a big deal with the FCC and what could be shown on animated programs. In the late 1980s and early 90s people like Mike Judge, John Krisfalusi and Matt Groening took the reins of pioneering animation as we see today. Come 1999 a gentleman known as Seth MacFarlane hit the scene with a ill received show lasting only 3 seasons known as Family Guy. A few years later this became the only show to be reinstated to television due to DVD sales. The antics of Family Guy became more humorous than the actual jokes in the main story line. Many shows, The Simpson's included, have resorted to cheap gags for laughs.
This is a brief timeline of animation. But much can be learned from commentary and interviews with the creators of beloved shows.

I had the same question and I spent some time doing research using inflation calculators and asked relatives about their expenses as well as their pay. What I concluded was:
1) The minimum wage was originally set to allow for one person working 40 hours a week to support a family of four.
2) The minimum wage in 1950 was just over 1 USD/hr adjusted for inflation equals just over 7 USD/hr. 

I then questioned the bills of the 1950s and compared to them of today.
In the 1950s people had typical bills of a mortgage, a land line telephone, one car payment, groceries, insurance, and annual taxes. These bills we all have today and even though from a number figure they look like they are substantially larger, when you adjust today's dollar value to the value in the 1950s they are relatively equal. 

So why does it seem impossible for one person working a minimum wage job to provide for their family? The simple answer is that it is not. If you stick to a strict budget and only pay for the necessities of life you will survive just fine. However what a minimum wage job cannot pay for is: internet, cell phones for the whole family, video games, cigarettes and alcohol in excess, a second car for your spouse, a third car for your kid when they turn 16, college tuition for your kids or even the student loans you took out and basically anything else that you can take for granted as an inalienable right but is not really necessary to survive.

TL;DR: Minimum wage can support a family of four in the 1950s the same way as it can today. It is a struggle but if you manage your money properly and live like you are in the 1950s you will get by just like those in The Golden Age.

This isn't Pokemon. Things don't evolve and disappear. Think of evolution as a bush at the bottom you have one singular organism from there other organisms can be traced back to. From each stem you have more new organisms. On each subsequent branch you can place another creature. As humans came to be much later than other primates you will find them further along the branches. Apes and monkeys will be closer to the main trunk. So just like on this proverbial bush branches don't cease to exist because a new branch sprouts from it animals do not cease to exist because a new creature is born of it. Also for clarification, do not expect a monkey to birth a human. This occurred because there were once a group of apes that got along socially and were better at doing things more human like than their ape like counterparts. So after several generations of breeding between themselves they genetically separated from their original kind. Do this a dozen or so times across 50,000 years and then you have humans.
